| [LIT-067](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-067.md) v2 | A Social Equilibrium Existence Theorem | Debreu (1952), DOI-10.1073/pnas.38.10.886. Debreu proves existence of an equilibrium for an "abstract economy" (generalized game), in which each agent's feasible set A_ι(ā_ι) depends on the others' actions. The conditions: each action set 𝔄_ι is a contractible polyhedron; A_ι has a closed graph with non-empty compact values; f_ι is continuous on the graph into the extended reals; the value function φ_ι(ā_ι) = max f_ι is continuous; and each best-response set M_ā_ι is contractible. The proof applies the Eilenberg–Montgomery/Begle fixed-point theorem to the product best-response map. A Remark replaces the joint continuity of φ_ι with continuity (lower hemicontinuity) of A_ι plus a compact graph. A Corollary gives a saddle-point theorem that contains Kakutani's and von Neumann's. | Active — read in full 2026-09-25 ([NOTE-037](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-037.md)); the original existence theorem for generalized (constrained) games, underlying Arrow–Debreu (1954). Short, fully self-contained, and still the canonical citation. Later results (Shafer–Sonnenschein 1975; the generalized-Nash literature) weaken its hypotheses but do not supersede it as the source. |

| [LIT-481](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-481.md) | Institutions, rules, and equilibria: a unified theory | Hindriks & Guala (2015, online 2014), DOI-10.1017/S1744137414000496. Institutions are rules in equilibrium: correlated equilibria of coordination games with several equilibria, which the players represent to themselves as rules. Searle's constitutive rules ("X counts as Y in C") are obtained from a regulative rule by splitting it with a new term, a base rule (X is Y) and a status rule (if Y then Z). The new term is conservative and eliminable, so the constitutive-rules account reduces to the rules-in-equilibrium account, and Lewis's theory of theoretical terms says the term refers if the rules are true. Shown on one toy institution (first-occupancy property); general reduction asserted. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-395](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-395.md)), with the authors' reply to their six commentators in the same issue; worth reading as the shortest statement of the rules-in-equilibrium theory of institutions and of the claim that Searle's constitutive rules are regulative rules with a name added. The equilibrium half is a clear synthesis of Lewis, Aumann, Aoki and Greif. The reduction of constitutive rules is shown on one toy institution and asserted in general, and it leans on a reading of "collective acceptance" loose enough to make it hard to fail. |

| [LIT-498](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-498.md) | The Evolution of Cooperation | Axelrod & Hamilton (1981), DOI-10.1126/science.7466396. In an iterated Prisoner's Dilemma with probability w of meeting again, TIT FOR TAT won two computer tournaments (14 and 62 entries) and an ecological simulation, and no strategy can do better against it when w ≥ max((T−R)/(T−P), (T−R)/(R−S)). ALL D is always stable; reciprocity can still enter through kinship or a cluster, after which a nice stable strategy resists clusters. Applications range from cleaner fish to disease and nondisjunction. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-411](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-411.md)); worth reading as the formal statement of how reciprocity can start, spread and hold: tit-for-tat is robust in Axelrod's tournaments, cannot be bettered by any mutant when the continuation probability w is high enough, and can enter an all-defect population through kinship or clustering. "Evolutionarily stable" is stronger than what is proved: the proof shows no strategy does better than TIT FOR TAT, and always-cooperate does as well, which Boyd & Lorberbaum (1987) later turned into a proof that no pure strategy is evolutionarily stable in the repeated game. It grounds the exchange domain of morality-as-cooperation; it is not about morality. |
| [LIT-501](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-501.md) | Five Rules for the Evolution of Cooperation | Nowak (2006), DOI-10.1126/science.1133755. Five mechanisms let natural selection favour cooperators who pay c to give b: kin selection (r > c/b), direct reciprocity (w > c/b), indirect reciprocity (q > c/b), network reciprocity (b/c > k) and group selection (b/c > 1 + n/m). Each is cast as a 2×2 game, from which conditions for cooperators to be evolutionarily stable, risk-dominant or advantageous follow. Punishment is said not to be a mechanism. Cooperation is proposed as a third principle of evolution. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-409](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-409.md)), main text only; the online supplement with the derivations was not read. Worth reading as the standard short map of mechanisms for the evolution of cooperation (kin selection, direct, indirect and network reciprocity, group selection), each reduced to a benefit-to-cost threshold from a 2×2 game. Every mechanism is modelled with the donation game, so it covers altruism only: mutualism, coordination and conflict resolution, four of morality-as-cooperation's seven domains, are outside it. Its one sentence on morality credits indirect reciprocity with "the evolution of morality", citing Alexander (1987). |

Morality is "a collection of biological and cultural solutions to the problems of cooperation and conflict recurrent in human social life". It reports no data. The seven domains are derived from game theory and then illustrated with quotations from philosophers and ethnographers, so the chapter shows the taxonomy is coherent, not that it is the right one. | [LIT-505](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-505.md) | The Logic of Animal Conflict | Maynard Smith & Price (1973), DOI-10.1038/246015a0. Why do animals with dangerous weapons fight conventionally? A simulation of five strategies (Mouse, Hawk, Bully, Retaliator, Prober-Retaliator) shows Hawk is not an evolutionarily stable strategy while Retaliator nearly is, so "limited war" can be favoured by individual selection. In a pure war of attrition no fixed persistence is stable; the ESS is an exponential mixture. There is no Hawk–Dove game and no ownership asymmetry here. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-404](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-404.md)); worth reading as the paper that introduced the evolutionarily stable strategy and showed that "limited war" in animal contests can be favoured by individual selection. It is not the source of the Hawk–Dove game or of owner–intruder conventions, though morality-as-cooperation cites it for both: its strategies are Mouse, Hawk, Bully, Retaliator and Prober-Retaliator, its contestants are symmetric, and its "Retaliator is an ESS" ties with Mouse, so it fails the paper's own second ESS condition. What it does ground for MAC's contest domains is restraint backed by retaliation, and, informally, retreat before a visibly superior opponent and honest signals of formidability. |

| [LIT-586](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-586.md) | Précis of Breakdown of Will | Ainslie (2005), Behavioral and Brain Sciences 28(5), the précis of Breakdown of Will (2001). People and other animals discount delayed rewards hyperbolically, so preferences reverse as a smaller, sooner reward comes near, and a person becomes a population of reward-seeking "interests" that must forestall one another. Willpower is the bundling of future choices by treating the present one as a precedent: an intertemporal repeated prisoner's dilemma, not an organ or a top-down ego. The same recursion predicts the will's costs: legalism, circumscribed "lapse districts", motivated blindness to lapses, and rules that favour countable goals over subtle ones. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-443](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-443.md)), as the substitute for the 2001 book ([LIT-583](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-583.md)), which the owner suggested and which the précis follows chapter by chapter. Worth reading as the shortest complete statement of picoeconomics in Ainslie's own words. Hyperbolic discounting makes preference reverse as a smaller, sooner reward draws near, so a person behaves like a population of "interests" that bargain across time. Will is not a faculty above them but a recursive self-prediction: treating each choice as a precedent "bundles" future rewards, an intertemporal repeated prisoner's dilemma in which "credibility is power". The same mechanism predicts the will's side effects: legalism, "lapse districts", motivated misperception and compulsive over-control. |
| [LIT-700](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-700.md) | Three kinds of collective attitudes | List (2014), Erkenntnis 79(S9):1601–1622. Collective attitudes come in three kinds. Aggregate attitudes summarise members' attitudes by a rule or a market, supervene proposition-wise and need not be rational. Common attitudes are held by all members with common awareness, matter for coordination, and inherit consistency from their unanimity. Corporate attitudes belong to a group agent, guide its action, supervene holistically on members' contributions and must be rational. The kinds are almost logically independent, and fears and hopes divide the same way as beliefs and desires. | Active — read in full 2026-10-04 ([NOTE-554](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-554.md)); worth reading as the disambiguation the collective-attitudes literature needs: aggregate attitudes (summaries, supervening proposition by proposition), common attitudes (unanimous and commonly known, supervening on a slightly enriched base) and corporate attitudes (a group agent's, supervening holistically and not straightforwardly reducible). The three are almost logically independent. A review by its own description, with no new theorem; its value for this record is that it names fears and hopes among the attitudes the split applies to, which gives the collective-emotion debate a vocabulary. |
| [LIT-719](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-719.md) | Beyond Markets and States: Polycentric Governance of Complex Economic Systems | Ostrom (2009), Nobel lecture; AER 2010. Polycentric arrangements of many formally independent decision centres can perform better than a single hierarchy. Worth reading as Ostrom's own summary of fifty years of work: polycentricity defined, the eight design principles of long-surviving common-pool resource institutions in their updated form, the experiments on communication and self-chosen sanctions, the field evidence on local monitoring, and the warning against single policy prescriptions. A retrospective lecture, not a report of new results. |
